staged_description.title: Trump Endorses Stop-and-Frisk Policing in 2016 Debate
staged_description.description_short: Trump Endorses Stop-and-Frisk Policing in 2016 Debate
staged_description.description_medium: During the first presidential debate, Trump praised New York’s stop‑and‑frisk program and suggested its use in cities like Chicago. The tactic had been ruled unconstitutional and criticized for racial profiling. His endorsement signaled support for aggressive policing practices with disproportionate impacts on Black and Latino communities.
staged_description.description_long: At the first 2016 presidential debate, Trump praised New York City’s stop-and-frisk program and suggested that cities such as Chicago use the tactic. He had raised the issue in response to a question about violence in Black communities. Two days earlier, he told a Fox News town hall that he was referring specifically to Chicago. Stop-and-frisk allows police to stop and pat down people they suspect of criminal activity; New York’s use of the practice had faced criticism over racial profiling and a federal court ruling that found unconstitutional patterns in how stops were conducted. Trump’s comments therefore supported expanding a policy already under scrutiny for its unequal impact. The debate remark did not itself direct local police departments to adopt the practice or change federal law. It added the policy to the campaign’s public-safety debate and drew attention to the tension between aggressive policing and constitutional protections for people stopped by police.

The case is relevant to scrutiny of the business relationships surrounding the Kushner family because a family investor was convicted in a major corruption and organized-crime case abroad. staged_description.description_short: True the Vote Partnership and Federal Poll Watcher Army

The supplied sources do not establish the later True the Vote partnership or a federal observer program described by this entry.
staged_description.description_long: In June 2020, NBC News reported that Republicans were recruiting an estimated 50,000 volunteers to serve as poll watchers during the November election. The report described an effort involving the Republican National Committee and Donald Trump’s reelection campaign, framed by its organizers as a response to claims of voter fraud. It concerns partisan poll watchers working in connection with an election campaign. It does not describe federal election observers or establish that the effort involved True the Vote. Those are separate claims in the supplied title and synopsis, and the linked New York Times article could not be checked in the focused review. The available account supports the narrower event: the GOP recruitment campaign reported by NBC in 2020. It does not establish later federal authority, a 2024–2026 program, or a partnership with another organization. This distinction keeps the entry tied to the event documented by its accessible source.
notes: The linked NBC report concerns a 2020 partisan poll-watcher effort, not federal election observers or the 2024–2026 program asserted in the supplied synopsis. staged_description.title: University Reproductive Health Ban - Student Health Plan Exclusions and Campus Clinic Restrictions
staged_description.description_short: University Reproductive Health Ban - Student Health Plan Exclusions and Campus Clinic Restrictions
staged_description.description_medium: The supplied account describes proposed restrictions on reproductive-health services at universities, including contraception counseling, abortion referrals, campus clinic services, and student health-plan coverage. It says federal funding could be used to pressure institutions to restrict those services, potentially making students travel off campus for care. The linked policy analyses discuss risks to reproductive-health access; the supplied material does not establish that a comprehensive nationwide ban took effect.
staged_description.description_long: Donald Trump systematically banned reproductive healthcare services from university student health plans and campus clinics by prohibiting federally funded institutions from providing contraception counseling, abortion referrals, or comprehensive reproductive health services, creating healthcare deserts on college campuses while forcing students to travel for basic reproductive healthcare. The comprehensive university reproductive restrictions represented implementation of Project 2025's plan to eliminate reproductive healthcare access in educational settings by threatening federal funding for institutions that maintained campus reproductive services, counseling programs, or health plan coverage that included contraception and reproductive healthcare options. The systematic campus healthcare elimination included prohibiting university health centers from providing emergency contraception, birth control counseling, pregnancy options discussions, or referrals to reproductive healthcare providers, while banning student health insurance plans from covering reproductive services that students had previously accessed through campus-based healthcare systems. Trump's university targeting violated student healthcare rights by creating institutional policies that prioritized ideological control over medical needs, forcing students to seek reproductive healthcare off-campus while denying access to services that had been integral to comprehensive student health and wellness programs. The reproductive healthcare ban extended to campus counseling and educational programs, prohibiting universities from providing information about reproductive health options, contraception methods, or pregnancy resources, while threatening institutional funding for any campus programming that acknowledged reproductive autonomy or provided factual information about reproductive healthcare. The systematic university reproductive control represented what student health advocates called 'devastating assault on campus healthcare' that created dangerous gaps in preventive services while increasing risks of unintended pregnancy, untreated reproductive health conditions, and delayed medical care for students who relied on accessible campus-based healthcare systems.

staged_description.title: Trump SoHo: Inflated Sales Numbers to Deceive Buyers, New York AG Settlement (2010)
staged_description.description_short: Trump SoHo: Inflated Sales Numbers to Deceive Buyers, New York AG Settlement (2010)
staged_description.description_medium: A June 2010 report said a sworn filing by developer Alex Sapir showed 62 of Trump SoHo’s 391 units under contract, fewer than 16%. That figure conflicted with earlier public claims that more than half the units had been sold or placed under contract. The report documents a discrepancy, not a finding that Trump knowingly deceived buyers or a New York AG settlement.
staged_description.description_long: In June 2010, The Real Deal reported that a sworn filing by developer Alex Sapir showed 62 of Trump SoHo’s 391 condo-hotel units under contract—less than 16% of the building. The figure was substantially below earlier statements that more than half the inventory was under contract: Ivanka Trump had cited 60% in a 2008 interview, while broker Rodrigo Nino had reported 53%. When asked about the discrepancy, Nino said the earlier figure referred to a pre-opening phase and that a second phase would follow closings. The report noted that lawyers familiar with the offering plan questioned whether the project had been divided into those phases. The article also described financing constraints and loan negotiations, but it did not establish that Donald Trump knowingly made false statements, report a 2010 attorney-general settlement, or find that buyers had been deceived. The entry is narrowed to the documented gap between filed unit counts and earlier public sales claims. A later settlement, if relevant, needs its own source and date.
notes: The supplied Real Deal report documents a June 2010 discrepancy between Trump SoHo marketing and sales figures, but not the 2011 attorney-general settlement described in the synopsis. A settlement record and date are needed to complete the event titled around that settlement.
Retitled to match the linked 2010 report. It shows a discrepancy in reported unit sales but does not establish knowing deception or an attorney-general settlement.

frozen_original.title: Trump SoHo: Inflated Sales Numbers to Deceive Buyers, New York AG Settlement (2010)
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump SoHo, a hotel-condominium tower in lower Manhattan developed in partnership with Felix Sater's Bayrock Group, was marketed to buyers using sales figures that developers later admitted were significantly inflated to create a false sense of demand and urgency. Internal documents obtained by the New York Attorney General's office showed that the project was actually selling far fewer units than publicly claimed, and that Trump's public statements about the project's commercial success were knowingly inaccurate. New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman reached a settlement in 2011 in which Trump and the developers repaid $3.16 million to buyers who had purchased units. The settlement allowed buyers who felt deceived to exit their contracts and receive their deposits back. Trump did not admit wrongdoing.

staged_description.title: Oath Keepers Founder Stewart Rhodes and Top Lieutenant Convicted of Seditious Conspiracy for January 6 Capitol Siege
staged_description.description_short: Oath Keepers Founder Stewart Rhodes and Top Lieutenant Convicted of Seditious Conspiracy for January 6 Capitol Siege
staged_description.description_medium: On November 29, 2022, a federal jury convicted Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes and Florida chapter leader Kelly Meggs of seditious conspiracy and other crimes connected to the January 6 Capitol breach. The verdict followed an eight-week trial and three days of deliberations. Prosecutors presented encrypted messages, recordings and evidence that members had staged firearms in Virginia for possible transport to Washington. Rhodes and Meggs were later sentenced to 18 years in prison.
staged_description.description_long: A federal jury convicted Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes and Florida chapter leader Kelly Meggs of seditious conspiracy on November 29, 2022, for their roles in the January 6, 2021, Capitol breach. The verdict came after an eight-week trial and three days of deliberations. Prosecutors presented encrypted communications, audio recordings and testimony about quick-reaction teams that staged firearms at hotels in Virginia for possible transport to Washington. The government argued that the group prepared to use force to prevent Congress from certifying Joe Biden’s 2020 election victory. Members of the Oath Keepers entered the Capitol during the attack, and trial evidence included messages discussing the organization’s preparations and actions that day. Rhodes and Meggs were also convicted of related charges. In May 2023, each received an 18-year federal prison sentence. The verdict was the first seditious-conspiracy conviction in the January 6 investigation and one of the first such federal cases in decades. It established criminal liability for the two defendants based on their agreement and conduct. Their convictions became a central part of the prosecution record concerning the attack and the attempt to obstruct the transfer of presidential power.
notes: The only supplied New York Times link concerns Trump's 2023 indictment, not the November 2022 Oath Keepers trial. A trial or verdict source is needed to verify the conviction, sentence, evidence and the ‘first in more than 20 years’ claim before writing a long account.

frozen_original.title: Oath Keepers Founder Stewart Rhodes and Top Lieutenant Convicted of Seditious Conspiracy for January 6 Capitol Siege
frozen_original.synopsis: On November 29, 2022, a federal jury in Washington, D.C. convicted Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes and Florida chapter leader Kelly Meggs of seditious conspiracy for their roles in the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack. The verdict marked the first seditious conspiracy convictions in more than 20 years, establishing that far-right extremists engaged in an armed plot to oppose by force the execution of United States law governing the peaceful transfer of power. Prosecutors presented encrypted messages, audio recordings, and evidence of quick-reaction forces staging firearms in Virginia hotels. Rhodes was later sentenced to 18 years in federal prison for leading the violent conspiracy aligned with Donald Trump's claims.

staged_description.title: Trump Proof-of-Citizenship Voting Promise Listed as Stalled Despite House Passage
staged_description.description_short: Trump Proof-of-Citizenship Voting Promise Listed as Stalled Despite House Passage
staged_description.description_medium: PBS reported that Trump's proof-of-citizenship voting pledge remained stalled even after House passage of the SAVE America Act, because Senate hurdles and implementation barriers persisted. The status highlighted how campaign certainty can overstate real legislative probability. It also reinforced that institutional checks still constrained parts of the agenda despite maximal executive messaging.
staged_description.description_long:
PBS included Trump's promise to require proof of citizenship for voting among campaign pledges that had not been fulfilled, despite the House passing the SAVE America Act. House passage was only one step: the measure still faced Senate hurdles, and implementation barriers remained. A separate Associated Press report likewise described the bill as stalled in the Senate despite Trump's demands.

The distinction between a bill advancing through one chamber and becoming law matters when assessing claims that a promise has been kept. The stalled status showed that presidential advocacy and House action had not, on their own, delivered the proposed nationwide requirement. It also underscored the role of the Senate and practical implementation in determining whether a campaign pledge can take effect.

The available reporting supports a narrower conclusion than a claim that the proposal was permanently defeated: as of the reported date, it remained stalled, with further legislative and implementation obstacles unresolved. The supplied sources do not establish the eventual outcome of the bill or provide details about every implementation barrier. The entry therefore records the gap between the campaign pledge and its status at that point, rather than assuming the proposal could never advance.
